lines.watchItem: Order visibility now runs to 2030 and your own tool demand is running about 1.9 times the level projected in December 2025, yet you still cannot meet current chip demand while building roughly 20 fabs at once. Watch whether construction labour and equipment delivery, rather than order intake, set how fast leading-edge wafer starts can rise.

Advanced-packaging allocation, not memory, is again named the binding limit on system availability, with lines quoted at roughly 52 to 78 weeks and capacity near 105,000 to 130,000 wafers a month by the fourth quarter of 2026. The exposure sits in how few buyers hold that booked capacity, because capacity freed by one of them is hard to refill.

Custom accelerator work keeps gaining ground on merchant parts: Broadcom booked $16.7 billion of artificial-intelligence chip revenue in its third quarter, up 221 percent year over year, and guides toward $115 billion in 2027 and $230 billion in 2028. At one leading model lab the largest single hardware obligation is about $161.2 billion of Broadcom equipment leases against up to $84.5 billion of Nvidia-based capacity, which shifts the leading-node customer base toward design houses and labs.

Scarcity still sets the price along the chain: the leading accelerator vendor can serve only about 70 percent of the demand it sees, one rental provider is raising on-demand rates 17 to 21 percent from October, and wafer price rises of 3 to 6 percent for 2027 are reported as planned. One memory supplier's chief executive already points to limited customer budgets, so watch whether buyer budgets start to cap that pass-through.

Memory is absorbing the budget and the wafers: its share of artificial-intelligence infrastructure spending is forecast to reach 57 percent by 2027 from 14 percent in 2025, and high-bandwidth memory is reported to take roughly three times the wafer capacity of ordinary memory. Stockpiles at the two largest suppliers sit below ten days, so any upset there lands directly on the accelerator builds your packaging slots are reserved for.

Second-source routes are widening around you: Intel is positioning a data-center inference part carrying up to 480 gigabytes of standard memory instead of high-bandwidth memory, SK Hynix is in early talks to make memory at Intel's Ohio plant, and OpenAI is deepening joint chip work with Samsung alongside the inference chip you already manufacture. Watch which of these turns into booked volume rather than announcement.

The committed capacity behind today's orders rests on money not yet earned: one model lab has set out at least $518 billion of infrastructure spending over a decade with about 80 percent non-cancelable, against a $42 billion net loss in 2025, while the largest cloud buyers are reported to sit about $125 billion a year short of break-even on their plans. Watch for the first slipped or renegotiated commitment, because wafer-start and packaging plans are sized against these books.

China exposure stays capped and policy-driven: the leading vendor's China revenue fell to $4.55 billion from $9.66 billion a year earlier, Beijing has signalled approval for a workstation-class part that one buyer is reported to plan a million units of, and the state plan targets 76 percent of Chinese chip demand met by domestic suppliers by 2030. Watch the licence terms, since they decide how much of that volume ever reaches your lines.
